lines.text: Beyond the window, a storm. Lightning looks like it strikes in an instant. It doesn't. The whole fall from the cloud takes tens of thousandths of a second. At this speed, that would take hours. So I'll skip ahead, and show you the highlights. First, a faint path of electric charge reaches down from the cloud, in jumps. Each jump is tens of meters long. Each takes about a microsecond. Here, one jump lasts one whole second. Then the path waits, about thirty to fifty microseconds. Here, that's half a minute or more. Then it jumps again, feeling its way down. Look at how it branches, like a tree turned upside down. At last it touches the ground, and a bright flash runs back up the three-kilometer path. That flash travels up to about a third of the speed of light. Even at a million times slower, it takes at least thirty seconds to climb. And that's the fastest thing so far. But it's still not light's top speed.
